overview: This file documents the mounting conflict in 1939–1940 between continued American commerce with Japan and efforts to deny Japan the materials and expertise needed for its war in China. Its records show the State Department administering a largely voluntary “moral embargo,” gathering company-level intelligence on exports, and deciding whether particular products or services—from aviation-fuel technology and petroleum additives to alloys, scrap metal, rubber, machinery, and minerals—fell within that policy. Corporate correspondence and trade statistics sit alongside diplomatic reporting, congressional inquiries, and petitions from churches, civic organizations, China-aid groups, and individual citizens. Collectively, the papers reveal an incremental and legally constrained transition from ordinary trade toward strategic economic pressure before the comprehensive sanctions of 1941.
interest: The file is especially useful for showing how an embargo developed transaction by transaction before it became a comprehensive national policy. Detailed corporate disclosures, technical discussions, and export statistics make it possible to reconstruct Japan’s dependence on American fuels, additives, metals, machinery, and industrial expertise, while internal memoranda expose the uncertain boundaries and uneven application of the voluntary restrictions. The petitions and congressional correspondence also illuminate the unusually broad coalition pressing the Roosevelt administration to act, as well as the Department’s repeated insistence that a general embargo required new statutory authority. For historians, the juxtaposition of commercial negotiations, bureaucratic deliberation, diplomatic intelligence, and moral protest offers a particularly rich view of the relationship between public opinion, private business, and foreign-policy formation.
